title: That to study philosophy is to learn to die
paragraphs: Cicero says "that to study philosophy is nothing but to prepare oneself to die." The reason is that study and contemplation in some sense withdraw the soul from us and employ it apart from the body — a kind of apprenticeship and resemblance of death; or else because all the wisdom and reasoning in the world finally come down to this one point: to teach us not to fear to die. To tell the truth, either our reason is mocking us, or it ought to have no other aim than our contentment, and to strive for nothing but, in sum, to make us live well and, as Holy Scripture says, at our ease. All the opinions of the world agree on this: that pleasure is our end, though we use various means to reach it. Otherwise they would all be rejected at the first move; for who would listen to anyone proposing affliction and misery as a final goal? The disputes between the philosophical sects on this point are merely verbal:
"Transcurramus solertissimas nugas"
["Let us skip over those subtle trifles." — Seneca, Ep., 117.]

— there is more in those quarrels of contention and obstinacy than is consistent with so sacred a profession; but whatever role a man takes upon himself to play, he always mixes in his own part with it.

Let the philosophers say what they will, the thing we all aim at, even in virtue, is pleasure. It amuses me to rattle in their ears this word that so nauseates them; and if it signifies some supreme pleasure and contentment, that is more owed to the help of virtue than to any other source. This pleasure, for being more cheerful, more sinewy, more robust, and more manly, is only the more seriously voluptuous, and we ought to give it the name of pleasure as the more favourable, gentle, and natural — not the lower form from which we have borrowed the word. The other and meaner pleasure, if it deserves this fair name at all, ought to have it by way of competition, not of privilege. I find it less exempt from troubles and inconveniences than virtue itself; and besides being more momentary, fluid, and frail in its enjoyment, it has its watchings, fasts, and labours, its sweat and its blood, and is afflicted besides with so many sharp and wounding passions, and so dull a satiety following on it, that it matches the severest penance. We mistake when we think these inconveniences serve only as a spur and seasoning to its sweetness (as in nature one contrary is quickened by its opposite), or say of virtue that the same difficulties overwhelm it and render it austere and inaccessible. On the contrary — much more aptly than in pleasure, those difficulties ennoble, sharpen, and heighten the perfect and divine pleasure that virtue procures for us. He renders himself unworthy of it who weighs its cost against its fruit, and neither understands the blessing nor how to use it. Those who preach to us that the quest of virtue is rocky, difficult, and painful but the enjoyment pleasant — what do they mean by that except to tell us virtue is always unpleasing? For by what human means is its enjoyment ever attained? The most perfect have had to content themselves with aspiring to it, and approaching it only, without ever possessing it. But they are mistaken: of all the pleasures we know, the very pursuit is pleasant. The attempt takes on the quality of the thing it is aimed at, for it is a good part of, and inseparable from, the effect. The happiness and blessedness that shine in virtue shine throughout all her approaches and avenues, even to the first entry and outermost limits.

Now, of all the benefits virtue confers on us, contempt of death is one of the greatest, because it is what fits human life with a soft and easy tranquillity, and gives us a pure and pleasant taste of living, without which all other pleasures would be extinguished. This is why all the rules centre and converge on this one article. And although they all likewise teach us, by common accord, to despise pain, poverty, and the other accidents human life is subject to, it is not with the same urgency — partly because those accidents are not so inevitable (the greater part of mankind pass their whole lives without ever knowing what poverty is, and some without sorrow or sickness, like Xenophilus the musician, who lived a hundred and six years in perfect and continual health); and partly because, at the worst, death can whenever we please cut short and put an end to all other inconveniences. But death itself is inevitable:
"Omnes eodem cogimur; omnium Versatur urna serius ocius Sors exitura, et nos in aeternum Exilium impositura cymbae."
["We are all bound one voyage; the lot of all, sooner or later, is to come out of the urn. All must sail away to eternal exile." — Hor., Od., ii. 3, 25.]

And consequently, if death frightens us, it is a perpetual torment for which there is no kind of consolation. There is no way by which it may not reach us. We may continually turn our heads this way and that, as in a country full of ambushes:
"Quae, quasi saxum Tantalo, semper impendet."
["Ever, like Tantalus' stone, it hangs over us." — Cicero, De Finib., i. 18.]
Our courts of justice often send condemned criminals back to be executed on the spot where the crime was committed; but on the way, take them to fine houses, lay on the best entertainment you can —
"Non Siculae dapes Dulcem elaborabunt saporem: Non avium cyatheaceae cantus Somnum reducent."
["Sicilian dainties will not tickle their palates, nor the melody of birds and harps bring back sleep." — Hor., Od., iii. 1, 18.]
Do you think they can enjoy any of it? Do you think the fatal end of their journey, constantly before their eyes, would not alter and spoil their taste for these delicacies?
"Audit iter, numeratque dies, spatioque viarum Metitur vitam; torquetur peste futura."
["He considers the route, counts the days of the journey, measures his life by the length of the road, and torments himself by thinking of the blow to come." — Claudianus, in Ruf., ii. 137.]

The end of our race is death. It is the necessary object of our aim, and if it frightens us, how is it possible to take a single step forward without a fit of fever? The remedy ordinary people use is not to think about it; but what brutish stupidity could produce so gross a blindness? They are trying to bridle the ass by the tail:
"Qui capite ipse suo instituit vestigia retro,"
["Who in his folly seeks to advance backwards." — Lucretius, iv. 474.]

No wonder he so often falls into the pit. They terrify people with the very word death, and many cross themselves as if at the name of the devil. And because making one's will refers to dying, no one can be persuaded to take up a pen for that purpose until the physician has passed sentence on him and given him over altogether; and then, between pain and terror, God knows in how fit a condition of understanding he is to do it.

The Romans, finding that this poor syllable death sounded so harshly to their ears and seemed so ominous, found a way to soften and spin it out by a circumlocution. Instead of saying "So-and-so is dead," they said "So-and-so has lived," or "So-and-so has ceased to live" — for, provided there was any mention of life in the phrase, even past life, it carried some sound of consolation. From them we borrowed our expression, "The late Monsieur So-and-so." Perhaps, as the saying goes, the words we have lived are worth our money. I was born between eleven and twelve o'clock in the forenoon on the last day of February 1533, by our reckoning, which begins the year on the 1st of January; and it is now just fifteen days since I turned thirty-nine years old, complete. I expect to live, at least, as many more. In the meantime, it would be folly to trouble myself with the thought of a thing so far off. But what? Young and old die on the same terms; no one leaves life otherwise than as if he had just entered it. And no man is so old and decrepit that, having heard of Methuselah, he does not think he has another twenty good years to come. Fool that you are! Who has guaranteed you the term of your life? You depend on physicians' tales: rather consult facts and experience. By the common course of things, you have for some time been living by extraordinary favour; you have already outlived the ordinary span. To prove it, count up your acquaintances and see how many more have died before reaching your age than have made it; and of those who ennobled their lives by their fame, just keep a tally, and I will lay you a wager you will find more who died before than after thirty-five. It is both reasonable and pious to take Jesus Christ Himself for an example: He ended His life at thirty-three. The greatest man who was no more than a man, Alexander, died also at the same age. How many ways death has to surprise us!
"Quid quisque, vitet, nunquam homini satis Cautum est in horas."
["Be as cautious as he may, no man can ever foresee the danger that may befall him at any hour." — Hor., Od., ii. 13, 13.]

To say nothing of fevers and pleurisies, who would ever have imagined that a Duke of Brittany would be crushed to death in a crowd, as that duke was at the entry of Pope Clement, my neighbour, into Lyons? Have you not seen one of our kings killed at a tilting match, and one of his ancestors die from being jostled by a hog? Aeschylus, warned of being killed by the fall of a house, took every possible precaution — and was knocked on the head by a tortoise dropped out of an eagle's talons in the air. Another man was choked by a grape-seed; an emperor was killed by the scratch of a comb while combing his hair. Aemilius Lepidus died by stumbling at his own threshold, and Aufidius by knocking against the door as he entered the council chamber. And between the very thighs of women: Cornelius Gallus the praetor; Tigillinus, captain of the watch at Rome; Ludovico, son of Guido di Gonzaga, Marquis of Mantua; and (a worse example) Speusippus, a Platonic philosopher, and one of our Popes. Poor Judge Bebius granted a postponement in a case for eight days; but in the meantime he himself was condemned by death, and his own stay of life expired. While Caius Julius the physician was anointing the eyes of a patient, death closed his own. And if I may bring in an example of my own blood: a brother of mine, Captain St. Martin, a young man of twenty-three who had already given sufficient proof of his courage, was playing a match at tennis when he received a blow from a ball a little above his right ear. As it left no sign of wound or bruise, he took no notice and did not even sit down to rest; nevertheless he died within five or six hours of an apoplexy caused by that blow.

With these frequent and ordinary examples passing every day before our eyes, how is it possible for a man to free himself from the thought of death, or to avoid fancying that it has us every moment by the throat? What does it matter, you will say, which way it comes, provided a man does not torment himself with the expectation? For my part, I am of this mind, and if a man could by any means avoid death — even by creeping under a calf's skin — I am one who would not be ashamed of the shift. All I aim at is to pass my time at my ease, and I take hold of whichever recreations contribute most to that, however little glorious or exemplary you may find them:
"Praetulerim . . . delirus inersque videri, Dum mea delectent mala me, vel denique fallant, Quam sapere, et ringi."
["I had rather seem mad and a sluggard, so long as my faults please me, or that I am not painfully aware of them, than be wise and snarling." — Hor., Ep., ii. 2, 126.]

But it is folly to think one can pull this off. They go, they come, they gallop and dance, and not a word of death. All very fine — but when it comes to themselves, their wives, their children, or their friends, surprising them off-guard and unprepared, what torment, what outcry, what madness and despair! Did you ever see anything so beaten down, so changed, so confounded? A man must therefore make earlier provision for it; and this brutish negligence — could it possibly lodge in the brain of any man of sense (which I think utterly impossible) — sells us its merchandise far too dearly. Were death an enemy that could be avoided, I would then advise borrowing arms even from cowardice itself; but since it cannot be avoided, and since it will catch you fleeing and playing the coward just as well as standing your ground like an honest man:
"Nempe et fugacem persequitur virum, Nec parcit imbellis juventae Poplitibus timidoque tergo."
["He pursues the fleeing coward, nor spares the hamstrings of the unwarlike youth who turns his back." — Hor., Ep., iii. 2, 14.]
And since no armour is proof against him:
"Ille licet ferro cautus, se condat et aere, Mors tamen inclusum protrahet inde caput"
["Let him hide beneath iron or brass in his fear, death will pull his head out of his armour." — Propertius, iii. 18.]

— let us learn to stand our ground bravely and fight him. And to begin to deprive him of the greatest advantage he has over us, let us take a way directly opposite to the common course. Let us disarm him of his novelty and strangeness, let us converse and be familiar with him, and have nothing so constantly in our thoughts as death. On every occasion let us picture him to our imagination in every shape: at the stumbling of a horse, at the falling of a tile, at the smallest prick of a pin, let us immediately consider and say to ourselves, "Well, and what if it had been death itself?" — and from there fortify and encourage ourselves. In the midst of our jollity and feasting, let us always set the remembrance of our frail condition before our eyes, never allowing ourselves to be so carried away by our pleasures that we have no intervals for reflecting on, and considering, how many ways this very jollity tends towards death, and with how many dangers it is shadowed. The Egyptians used to do this: at the height of their feasting and mirth, they would have a dried human skeleton brought into the room as a memento to their guests:
"Omnem crede diem tibi diluxisse supremum Grata superveniet, quae non sperabitur, hora."
["Think every day, when it is over, your last; the next, as unhoped-for, will be the more welcome." — Hor., Ep., i. 4, 13.]

Where death waits for us is uncertain; let us look for him everywhere. The premeditation of death is the premeditation of liberty. He who has learned to die has unlearned to be a slave. There is nothing evil in life for him who rightly understands that the loss of life is no evil; to know how to die delivers us from all subjection and constraint. Paulus Aemilius answered the man whom the wretched King of Macedon, his prisoner, had sent to beg him not to lead him in his triumph: "Let him make that request to himself."

In truth, in all things, if nature does not help a little, it is very hard for art and effort to accomplish much to the purpose. I am not by nature melancholy, but meditative; and there is nothing I have entertained myself with more continually than imaginations of death — even in the most carefree time of my youth:
"Jucundum quum aetas florida ver ageret."
["When my flowering age rejoiced in pleasant spring." — Catullus, lxviii.]

In the company of ladies, and at games, some have perhaps thought me preoccupied with some jealousy, or the uncertainty of some hope, when in fact I was entertaining myself with the memory of someone caught up, a few days earlier, by a burning fever of which he died, returning from an entertainment like this one with his head full of idle fancies of love and merriment, as mine then was — and that, for all I knew, the same destiny might be waiting for me.
"Jam fuerit, nec post unquam revocare licebit."
["Soon the present will have gone, never to be called back." — Lucretius, iii. 928.]

Yet such a thought did not wrinkle my forehead any more than another did. It is impossible not to feel a sting in such imaginings at first; but with often turning and returning them in one's mind, they finally become so familiar as to be no trouble at all. Otherwise, for my part, I should be in perpetual fright and frenzy; for no man was ever more distrustful of his life than I, nor more uncertain as to its duration. Neither the health I have so far enjoyed — strong and vigorous, and very seldom interrupted — prolongs my expectations, nor does sickness shorten them. Every minute, it seems to me, I am escaping; and the thought constantly runs through my mind that what may be done tomorrow may be done today. Hazards and dangers do, in truth, little or nothing to hasten our end; and if we consider how many thousands more hang over our heads besides the accident that immediately threatens us, we shall find that the healthy and the sick, those at sea and those by the fire, those engaged in battle and those sitting idle at home, are all equally near to it.
"Nemo altero fragilior est; nemo in crastinum sui certior."
["No man is more fragile than another; no man more certain than another of tomorrow." — Seneca, Ep., 91.]
For whatever I have to do before I die, the longest leisure would seem too short, even if it were only an hour's business I had on hand.

A friend of mine, the other day, leafing through my tablets, found there a note of something I wanted done after my death; I told him, and it was the truth, that though I was no more than a league from home, well and merry, when the thing came into my head I had hurried to write it down there, because I was not certain to live till I came home. As a man eternally brooding over his own thoughts, and confining them to his own particular concerns, I am at all hours as well prepared as I am ever likely to be; and death, whenever he comes, can bring nothing along with him that I have not been expecting for a long time. We should always, as nearly as we can, be booted and spurred and ready to go; and above all things, at that hour, take care to have no business with anyone but ourselves:
"Quid brevi fortes jaculamur avo Multa?"
["Why for so brief a life tease ourselves with so many projects?" — Hor., Od., ii. 16, 17.]

For we shall there find work enough to do, without any need of addition. One man complains, more than of death, that he is by it prevented from a glorious victory; another, that he must die before he has married off his daughter or educated his children; a third regrets only the loss of his wife's company; a fourth, the conversation of his son, as the chief comfort and concern of his life. For my part, I am — thanks be to God — at this moment in such a state that I am ready to move on whenever it shall please Him, without regret for anything whatsoever. I disengage myself completely from all worldly relations; my leave is soon taken of all but myself. Never did anyone prepare to say goodbye to the world more absolutely and unreservedly, or shake hands more completely with all interest in it, than I expect to do. The deadest deaths are the best:
"'Miser, O miser,' aiunt, 'omnia ademit Una dies infesta mihi tot praemia vitae.'"
["'Wretch that I am,' they cry, 'one fatal day has deprived me of all the joys of life.'" — Lucretius, iii. 911.]
And the builder,
"Manuet," says he, "opera interrupta, minaeque Murorum ingentes."
["The works remain unfinished, the tall pinnacles of the walls unmade." — Aeneid, iv. 88.]
A man should plan nothing that will need so much time to finish — or at least, with no such passionate desire to see it through to perfection. We are born to action:
"Quum moriar, medium solvar et inter opus."
["When I shall die, let me be in the midst of what I had designed." — Ovid, Amor., ii. 10, 36.]

I would always have a man busy, and, as far as in him lies, extending and spinning out the offices of life; and then let death take me planting my cabbages, indifferent to him and still less troubled that my garden is not finished. I once saw a man die who, at his last gasp, complained of nothing so much as that destiny was about to cut the thread of a chronicle he was then compiling, and he was only as far as the fifteenth or sixteenth of our kings:
"Illud in his rebus non addunt: nec tibi earum jam desiderium rerum super insidet una."
["They do not add this: that dying, the desire for those things no longer hangs about us." — Lucretius, iii. 913.]

We must disengage ourselves from these common and hurtful humours. It was for this reason that men first placed cemeteries adjoining the churches, and in the most frequented parts of the city — to accustom, says Lycurgus, the common people, women, and children, so they should not be startled at the sight of a corpse; and that the continual sight of bones, graves, and funeral rites should keep us mindful of our frail condition:
"Quin etiam exhilarare viris convivia caede Mos olim, et miscere epulis spectacula dira Certantum ferro, saepe et super ipsa cadentum Pocula, respersis non parco sanguine mensis."

["It was formerly the custom to enliven banquets with slaughter, and to combine with the meal the dire spectacle of men contending with the sword — the dying often falling upon the cups and covering the tables with blood." — Silius Italicus, xi. 51.]

And as the Egyptians, after their feasts, used to present the company with a great image of death, while one cried out to them, "Drink and be merry, for such you shall be when you are dead," so it is my custom to have death not only in my imagination but continually in my mouth. There is nothing I am so curious to inform myself of as the manner of men's deaths — their words, their looks, their bearing; nor any passages in history I am so intent upon. It is plain enough, by my crowding in examples of this kind, that I have a particular fancy for the subject. If I were a writer of books, I would compile a register, with commentary, of the various deaths of men: he who would teach men to die would at the same time teach them to live. Dicaearchus made one and gave it that title, but designed it for a different and less profitable end.

Perhaps someone will object that the pain and terror of dying so infinitely exceed all imagination, that the best fencer will be quite out of his play when it comes to the push. Let them say what they will: to premeditate is no doubt a very great advantage; and besides, is it nothing to go so far, at least, without disturbance or alteration? Moreover, Nature herself helps and encourages us. If death is sudden and violent, we have no leisure to fear it; if otherwise, I notice that, as I sink further into my illness, I naturally fall into a certain loathing and disdain of life. I find I have much more trouble digesting the thought of dying when I am in good health than when I am languishing of a fever; and the less hold I have on the comforts of life — beginning to lose the use and pleasure of them — the less terror I feel at death. This makes me hope that the further I get from the first state, and the nearer I come to the second, the more easily I shall exchange the one for the other. And just as I have found in other matters, as Caesar says, that things often appear greater to us at a distance than close at hand, I have found that, being well, I have held maladies in much greater horror than when really afflicted with them. The vigour I am in now, the cheerfulness and delight in which I now live, make the contrary state appear in so great a disproportion to my present condition that, by imagination, I magnify those inconveniences by half, and apprehend them to be much more troublesome than I actually find them to be when they lie heaviest upon me. I hope to find death the same.

Let us only observe, in the ordinary changes and declinations we daily undergo, how nature deprives us of the awareness and sense of our bodily decay. What remains to an old man of the vigour of his youth, of his better days?
"Heu! senibus vitae portio quanta manet."
["Alas, what a small portion of life remains to old men!" — Maximian, or Pseudo-Gallus, i. 16.]

Caesar, to an old, weather-beaten soldier of his guard who came to ask leave to kill himself, taking notice of his withered body and decrepit movements, answered pleasantly, "You fancy, then, that you are still alive?" Should a man fall suddenly into this condition, I do not think human nature capable of enduring such a change; but nature, leading us by the hand at an easy and almost imperceptible pace, step by step conducts us into that miserable state and so makes it familiar, that we feel no shock when our youth dies in us, though it is really a harder death than the final dissolution of a languishing body — than the death of old age. For the fall is not so great from an uneasy being to none at all as it is from a sprightly and flourishing being to one that is troublesome and painful. The body, bent and bowed, has less force to support a burden; and it is the same with the soul. We must therefore raise her up firm and erect against the power of this adversary. For so long as she stands in fear of him, she can never be at rest; but if she can once assure herself, she may boast — a thing almost surpassing the human condition — that anxiety, disquiet, fear, or any other disturbance is incapable of inhabiting or having any place in her:
"Non vulnus instants Tyranni Mentha cadi solida, neque Auster Dux inquieti turbidus Adriae, Nec fulminantis magna Jovis manus."

["Not the threatening look of a tyrant shakes her well-settled mind, nor the turbulent Auster, prince of the stormy Adriatic, nor the great hand of thundering Jove — such a temper they cannot move." — Hor., Od., iii. 3, 3.]

She has then become sovereign over all her lusts and passions, mistress of necessity, of shame, of poverty, and of all the other injuries of fortune. Let us, then, as many as can, gain this advantage; it is the true and sovereign liberty here on earth, that fortifies us to defy violence and injustice, and to despise prisons and chains:
"In manicis et Compedibus saevo te sub custode tenebo. Ipse Deus, simul atque volam, me solvet. Opinor, Hoc sentit; moriar; mors ultima linea rerum est."
["I will keep you in fetters and chains, under a savage keeper. — A god, when I ask Him, will set me free. This god, I think, is death. Death is the end of all things." — Hor., Ep., i. 16, 76.]

Our very religion has no surer human foundation than the contempt of life. Not only does reason invite us to it — for why should we fear to lose a thing which, being lost, cannot be lamented? — but, also, since we are threatened by so many sorts of death, is it not infinitely worse to fear them all eternally than to undergo one of them once? And what does it matter when it comes, since it is inevitable? To the man who told Socrates, "The thirty tyrants have sentenced you to death," he replied, "And nature them." What a ridiculous thing it is to trouble ourselves about taking the one step that delivers us from all trouble! As our birth brought us the birth of all things, so our death includes the death of all things. Therefore to lament that we shall not be alive a hundred years hence is the same folly as to be sorry we were not alive a hundred years ago. Death is the beginning of another life. So did we weep, and so much did it cost us, to enter into this one, and so did we put off our former veil in entering it. Nothing can be a grievance that happens only once. Is it reasonable to be afraid for so long of a thing that will be dispatched so quickly? Long life and short are by death made all one; for there is no long, nor short, for things that are no more. Aristotle tells us there are certain little creatures on the banks of the river Hypanis that live no more than a day: those which die at eight in the morning die young, and those that die at five in the evening die in their decrepitude. Which of us would not laugh to see this moment of existence treated as a matter of weal or woe? The most and the least of ours, in comparison with eternity, or even with the duration of mountains, rivers, stars, trees, and some animals, is no less ridiculous.

But nature compels us to it. "Go out of this world," she says, "as you entered it. The same passage you made from death to life, without passion or fear — make the same again, in the same way, from life to death. Your death is part of the order of the universe; it is part of the life of the world.
"Inter se mortales mutua vivunt ................................ Et, quasi cursores, vitai lampada tradunt."
["Mortals, amongst themselves, live by turns, and, like the runners in the games, give up the lamp, when they have won the race, to the next comer." — Lucretius, ii. 75, 78.]

"Shall I alter this beautiful arrangement of things for you? It is the condition of your creation. Death is a part of you, and while you try to evade it, you evade yourselves. This very being of yours that you now enjoy is equally divided between life and death. The day of your birth is one day's advance towards the grave:
"Prima, qux vitam dedit, hora carpsit."
["The first hour that gave us life took away also an hour of it." — Seneca, Her. Fur., 3 Chor. 874.]
"Nascentes morimur, finisque ab origine pendet."
["As we are born we die, and the end commences with the beginning." — Manilius, Ast., iv. 16.]

"All the time you live, you steal from life and live at the expense of life itself. The perpetual work of your life is but to lay the foundation of death. You are in death while you are in life, because you still are after death, when you are no longer alive — or, if you prefer it the other way, you are dead after life, but dying all the while you live; and death handles the dying much more roughly than the dead, and more sensibly and essentially. If you have made profit of life, you have had enough of it; go your way satisfied.
"Cur non ut plenus vita; conviva recedis?"
["Why not depart from life as a sated guest from a feast?" — Lucretius, iii. 951.]
"If you have not known how to make the best use of it, if it was no good to you, what need have you to care about losing it? Why would you want to keep it longer?
"'Cur amplius addere quaeris, Rursum quod pereat male, et ingratum occidat omne?'
["Why seek to add longer life, merely to renew ill-spent time and be again tormented?" — Lucretius, iii. 914.]

"Life in itself is neither good nor evil; it is the scene of good or evil as you make it.' And if you have lived a day, you have seen all: one day is equal and like all other days. There is no other light, no other shade; this very sun, this moon, these very stars, this very order and arrangement of things, is the same your ancestors enjoyed, and shall also entertain your posterity:
"'Non alium videre patres, aliumve nepotes Aspicient.'
["Your grandsires saw no other thing; nor will your posterity." — Manilius, i. 529.]

"And, come the worst that can come, the distribution and variety of all the acts of my comedy are played out in a year. If you have observed the revolution of my four seasons, they contain the infancy, the youth, the manhood, and the old age of the world. The year has played its part, and knows no other art but to begin again. It will always be the same thing:
"'Versamur ibidem, atque insumus usque.'
["We are turning in the same circle, ever confined within it." — Lucretius, iii. 1093.]
"'Atque in se sua per vestigia volvitur annus.'
["The year is ever turning around in the same footsteps." — Virgil, Georg., ii. 402.]
"I am not prepared to create for you any new diversions:
"'Nam tibi prxterea quod machiner, inveniamque Quod placeat, nihil est; eadem sunt omnia semper.'
["I can devise, nor find, anything else to please you: it is the same thing over and over again." — Lucretius, iii. 957.]

"Give place to others, as others have given place to you. Equality is the soul of equity. Who can complain of being included in the same fate that all are involved in? Besides, live as long as you can — you shall by that not shorten by a moment the span you are to be dead; it is all to no purpose. You shall be as long in the condition you so much fear as if you had died at the breast:
"'Licet quot vis vivendo vincere secla, Mors aeterna tamen nihilominus illa manebit.'
["Live triumphing over as many ages as you will, death will still remain eternal." — Lucretius, iii. 1103.]
"And yet I will place you in such a condition that you shall have no reason to be displeased.
"'In vera nescis nullum fore morte alium te, Qui possit vivus tibi to lugere peremptum, Stansque jacentem.'
["Do you not know that, when dead, there can be no other living self to lament you dead, standing over your grave." — Idem., ibid., 898.]
"Nor will you so much as wish for the life you are now so concerned about:
"'Nec sibi enim quisquam tum se vitamque requirit. .................................................. "'Nec desiderium nostri nos afficit ullum.'
"Death is less to be feared than nothing, if there could be anything less than nothing.
"'Multo . . . mortem minus ad nos esse putandium, Si minus esse potest, quam quod nihil esse videmus.'

"Nor can it concern you, in any way, whether you are living or dead: living, because you are still in being; dead, because you are no more. Moreover, no one dies before his hour: the time you leave behind was no more yours than the time that lapsed and went by before you came into the world, nor does it any more concern you.
"'Respice enim, quam nil ad nos anteacta vetustas Temporis aeterni fuerit.'
["Consider how the old age of times past is as nothing to us." — Lucretius, iii. 985.]

Wherever your life ends, it is all there. The use of living lies not in the length of days, but in the use of time; a man may have lived long and yet lived little. Make use of time while it is present with you. It depends on your will, and not on the number of days, to have a sufficient length of life. Is it possible you imagine you will never arrive at the place towards which you are continually going? And yet there is no journey but has its end. And if company will make it more pleasant or easier for you, does not all the world go the very same way?
"'Omnia te, vita perfuncta, sequentur.'
["All things, then, life over, must follow you." — Lucretius, iii. 981.]

"Does not all the world dance the same dance you do? Is there anything that does not grow old, as well as you? A thousand men, a thousand animals, a thousand other creatures die the same moment you die:
"'Nam nox nulla diem, neque noctem aurora sequuta est, Quae non audierit mistos vagitibus aegris Ploratus, mortis comites et funeris atri.'
["No night has followed day, no day has followed night, in which there have not been heard sobs and sorrowing cries, the companions of death and dark funerals." — Lucretius, v. 579.]

"To what purpose should you try to draw back, if there is no way to evade it? You have seen plenty of examples of those who were well content to die, as thereby delivered from heavy miseries; but have you ever found any who were dissatisfied with dying? It must therefore be very foolish to condemn a thing you have not experienced either in your own person or in anyone else's. Why do you complain of me and of destiny? Do we do you any wrong? Is it for you to govern us, or for us to govern you? Though, perhaps, your years are not complete, yet your life is. A man of small stature is as much a man as a giant; neither men nor their lives are measured by the yard. Chiron refused to be immortal when he was told the conditions on which he was to enjoy it, by the god of time itself and its duration, his father Saturn. Just seriously consider how much more unbearable and painful an immortal life would be to man than the life I have already given him. If you had not death, you would eternally curse me for having deprived you of it. I have mixed a little bitterness with it, so that, seeing how convenient it is, you might not too greedily and indiscreetly seek to embrace it; and so that you might be so settled in this moderation as neither to be sick of life nor to have any antipathy for dying — which I have decreed you shall do once — I have tempered both of them between pleasure and pain. It was I that taught Thales, the most eminent of your sages, that to live and to die were indifferent, which made him, very wisely, answer the man who asked him why he did not die: 'Because,' he said, 'it is indifferent.' Water, earth, air, and fire, and the other parts of this creation of mine, are no more instruments of your life than they are of your death. Why do you fear your last day? It contributes no more to your dissolution than every one of the rest. The last step is not the cause of your weariness; it only declares it. Every day travels towards death; the last only arrives at it." These are the good lessons our mother Nature teaches.

I have often wondered why it should be that in war the image of death, whether we look at it in ourselves or in others, appears, beyond comparison, less dreadful than at home in our own houses (for if it were not so, the army would be made up of doctors and whining milksops); and that, since death is the same in all places, there should nevertheless be much more steadiness in peasants and common people than in those of higher rank. I truly believe it is those terrible ceremonies and preparations we surround it with that frighten us more than the thing itself: a new, quite contrary way of living; the cries of mothers, wives, and children; the visits of stunned and grieving friends; the attendance of pale and snivelling servants; a dark room set round with burning tapers; our beds surrounded by physicians and priests — in sum, nothing but ghostliness and horror around us. We seem dead and buried already. Children are afraid even of those they know best, when disguised behind a mask; and so it is with us. The mask must be removed from things as well as from persons; once it is taken away, we shall find underneath nothing but the very same death that a mean servant or a poor chambermaid died a day or two ago, without any kind of apprehension. Happy is the death that deprives us of leisure for preparing such ceremonials.
